linkedin.hook: A transcript is not a content plan. It is one argument buried under every repeated sentence.
linkedin.body:
You already did the hard part. You recorded the teardown, the client call, or the talk. The waste starts when that transcript gets pasted into a feed and called a post.

Pull one argument out. Say it in a sentence a stranger can repeat. Then give each channel a job instead of a shorter copy of the same blob.

LinkedIn carries the argument, one concrete moment, and a reason to reply. A thread carries the claim in pieces a phone can hold, and it does not open with a number. The newsletter is where the teaching goes, because those people asked for the long version. The short video is one breath: a hook, three beats, words on screen, and a close that names the next step.

If a draft breaks a length rule, the draft is wrong. Fix it before you hit publish.

sections.heading: Find the sentence
sections.body: Read the transcript once and write the single claim a stranger could repeat. If you cannot find it, you do not have a post yet. You have notes.

sections.heading: Give each channel a job
sections.body: LinkedIn argues. The thread slices the claim. The newsletter teaches. The short video is the hook and the close. Same argument, four shapes, no pasted transcript.

beats.spoken: Stop posting the transcript. A transcript is one argument buried under every time you said the same thing twice.
Pull that argument into one sentence a stranger can use. LinkedIn gets the argument and one concrete moment. The thread gets the claim in pieces. The newsletter is where you teach.
The short version is this breath. Hook, three beats, words on screen, and a close that tells people what to do next. If the draft is too long, cut the draft.
